lesson.title: The Bandwidth You Don't Get for Free
lesson.summary: Real op-amps trade gain for bandwidth according to a fixed gain-bandwidth product, so cranking up the closed-loop gain always shrinks how much of the frequency spectrum the amplifier can faithfully pass.
lesson.body:
The ideal op-amp model treats open-loop gain as infinite at every frequency, which is why the closed-loop gain equations from earlier chapters (like Rf/Rg for an inverting amplifier) work out to clean, frequency-independent numbers. A real op-amp cannot do that. Internally it has a dominant capacitor, placed there on purpose to keep the amplifier stable, that causes the open-loop gain to roll off as frequency increases, starting from a corner frequency that is often just tens of hertz. Above that corner, gain falls at a steady rate as frequency climbs.

Despite that rolloff, something stays constant across most of the useful range: the product of open-loop gain and frequency. Multiply the gain at any point on the rolloff by the frequency at that point and you get roughly the same number every time. That constant is called the gain-bandwidth product, or GBW, and every op-amp datasheet lists it, usually in megahertz.

GBW sets a hard limit on closed-loop bandwidth. Because feedback can only work with whatever open-loop gain is actually available at a given frequency, the closed-loop bandwidth of an amplifier configured for gain A_CL comes out to approximately f_BW = GBW / A_CL. Configure the op-amp for a small gain and it stays accurate out to a high frequency. Configure it for a large gain and that same amplifier's useful frequency range shrinks proportionally.

Here is the tradeoff worked out with real numbers. Take an op-amp with GBW = 1 MHz, typical of an everyday general-purpose part. Build a non-inverting amplifier with Rf = 99 kΩ and Rg = 1 kΩ, giving a closed-loop gain of 1 + 99k/1k = 100. The closed-loop bandwidth is then approximately 1,000,000 Hz / 100 = 10,000 Hz, or 10 kHz. Now double the feedback resistor to Rf = 199 kΩ. Gain becomes 1 + 199k/1k = 200, and bandwidth drops to 1,000,000 / 200 = 5,000 Hz, or 5 kHz. Doubling the gain exactly halved the bandwidth, which is the GBW tradeoff in action.

This has a direct, practical consequence when choosing a part. Suppose an audio circuit needs a flat response out to 20 kHz at a gain of 50. The minimum required GBW is 20 kHz times 50, which is 1,000,000 Hz, or 1 MHz. A 1 MHz GBW op-amp only just meets that number, and since f_BW = GBW/A_CL is the point where the response has already fallen 3 dB, a part rated at exactly 1 MHz would deliver a badly drooping response at 20 kHz rather than a flat one. Real designs build in margin, typically choosing an op-amp with 5 to 10 times the bare minimum GBW, so 5 to 10 MHz, to keep the response flat well past the frequency of interest.
